prompt.context: It is October 2001, and our client is the New York City Economic Development Corporation (EDC). The EDC partners with a variety of governmental and non-governmental firms, serving as an engine for economic development. The EDC is charged with leveraging the city's assets to drive growth, create jobs and improve quality of life. Like a Chamber of Commerce, the EDC shapes policy for local business interests. The EDC is requesting our help in looking at the city's hotel industry in the wake of the September 11th attacks.
prompt.question:
1. Can we quantify the expected impact of 9/11 on the New York City hotel industry?
2. Will the New York City hotel industry need government assistance?

clarifying_info.q: What kind of assistance does the EDC provide, or what kinds of policies does it try to influence?
clarifying_info.a: What do you think the EDC could do to advance local business interests? (e.g., lobbying for tax changes to stimulate purchases from local businesses)

clarifying_info.q: Are we talking about all of New York City or just Manhattan?
clarifying_info.a: We are considering all five boroughs.

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue breakdown or cost structure for the NYC hotel industry?
clarifying_info.a: We will get there — please build your framework first.

framework: Part 1 — Profitability of the NYC hotel industry BEFORE 9/11: Revenue (rooms × occupancy × rate) and Costs (fixed: property, wages/salaries, insurance, utilities; variable: room service, laundry, etc.)

Part 2 — Modeled profitability AFTER 9/11: Adjust revenue down by segment (business vs. leisure travelers), keep room rates flat short-term, recalculate costs given new occupancy, derive new profit (or loss)
Recommendation — Based on the magnitude of the profitability swing, assess whether the industry needs government assistance and what form that assistance should take

questions.prompt: Calculate the nightly revenue for the NYC hotel industry before 9/11.
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask about number of hotels, rooms per hotel, occupancy rate, and average room rate. Strong candidates note the business vs. leisure traveler split as a useful segmentation for later.

math.setup: Nightly Revenue = # hotels × rooms/hotel × occupancy rate × average rate
steps: 75,000 rooms × 80% occupancy = 60,000 occupied rooms per night

questions.prompt: Estimate nightly costs and profit for the NYC hotel industry before 9/11. What is the FC/VC breakdown?
questions.guidance: No cost data is provided; candidate must make assumptions. Interviewer steers toward a 10% profit margin. Candidate should also establish FC vs. VC split, recognizing the hotel industry has high fixed costs.

math.setup: Assume 10% profit margin → costs = 90% of revenue. Assume 80% of costs are fixed, 20% variable.
math.answer: Nightly profit ≈ $1.8M; Fixed costs ≈ $13M/night; Variable costs ≈ $3.2M/night

questions.prompt: Model the change in profitability after 9/11. What revenue and costs should we expect in the short term?
questions.guidance: Candidate must make assumptions — no data is given. Reasonable assumptions: 50/50 business/leisure split before 9/11; leisure travelers stop coming entirely; 50% of business travelers cancel; room rates unchanged at $300. Fixed costs stay constant; variable costs drop proportionally to occupancy. Target answer range is ($5M) to ($12M) nightly loss.

math.setup: Revised revenue: leisure revenue = $0; business revenue = 25% of original (50% of travelers × 50% still traveling). Fixed costs unchanged; variable costs scale with occupancy.
steps: Pre-9/11 leisure revenue = $9M, post-9/11 leisure revenue = $0
Pre-9/11 business revenue = $9M; 50% of business travelers remain → business revenue = $9M × 25% = $4.5M (only 25% of all rooms now occupied by business travelers)
Variable costs scale: $3.2M ÷ 4 = $800K per night (occupancy dropped to ~25% of original)
math.answer: Nightly loss ≈ ($9.3M); range of ($5M) to ($12M) is acceptable depending on assumptions

questions.prompt: Given this analysis, does the NYC hotel industry need government assistance? How can the EDC help?
questions.guidance: Candidate should strongly conclude that the industry needs help given the massive daily losses. Should brainstorm government levers across federal, state, and local levels. Strong candidates differentiate between chains (can sustain losses via other locations) and independent hotels. They should also note geographic variation in impact (proximity to Financial District/Twin Towers) and that some hotels may be temporarily uninhabitable.

brainstorming.prompt: What could the EDC (and government more broadly) do to help the NYC hotel industry?

categories.name: Financial relief
ideas: Tax breaks or tax deferrals for hotels
Direct federal or state funding/grants to individual hotels

categories.name: Demand stimulation
ideas: PR/marketing blitz to incentivize domestic tourism to NYC
Government-sponsored campaigns to restore confidence in NYC travel
Partnering with airlines to offer discounted travel packages

categories.name: Operational support
ideas: Use vacant hotel rooms to house first responders and rescue workers at Ground Zero
Coordinate with FEMA to house displaced residents
Temporary waivers of hotel regulatory requirements to reduce operating costs

categories.name: Structural/policy levers
ideas: Lobby for federal disaster relief legislation specific to NYC businesses
Facilitate access to SBA emergency loans
Work with unions to temporarily renegotiate labor agreements

categories.name: Differentiated support by hotel type
ideas: Independent hotels may need more direct aid than chain hotels (chains generate revenue elsewhere)
Hotels near the Financial District may need priority assistance
Hotels that are temporarily uninhabitable need separate treatment

recommendation: Yes, 9/11 will have a severe and quantifiable impact on the NYC hotel industry — the industry will swing from approximately $1.8M nightly profit to approximately ($9.3M) nightly loss, a swing of over $11M per night

The industry will almost certainly need government assistance, particularly independent hotels and those nearest Ground Zero, as the high fixed-cost structure means even a short-term demand shock creates devastating losses
risks: Government assistance may create dependency or delay necessary industry restructuring
A PR campaign may be premature if public safety concerns are not yet fully resolved
Chain hotels may not need the same level of support as independent hotels — blanket policies could be inefficient
next_steps: Gather data on current financial health (cash reserves, debt levels) of hotels to size the assistance needed
Differentiate support programs by hotel type (chain vs. independent) and geography (proximity to Ground Zero)
Model how long the demand shock is expected to last and what recovery scenarios look like
Identify which level of government (federal, state, local) is best positioned to deliver each type of assistance
